newsitem.title: THAILAND: Beyond IMF, Thailand faces bumpy political month.
newsitem.headline: Beyond IMF, Thailand faces bumpy political month.

text.p: Thailand faces fallout from its economic crisis as well as deepening political uncertainty, heralding a difficult month ahead, analysts, academics and newspapers said on Tuesday.

Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh, known for oblique statements, was quoted by Tuesday's newspapers as promising political change after the government finalises an economic rescue package with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) later this month.
Chavalit declined to be more specific, leaving many guessing about either a reshuffle, an election, or something more dramatic.
"The government as it stands is not going to last. It will remain in place until the IMF deal is signed, sealed and delivered," one Bangkok-based foreign analyst said.
"After that we will see some political change but what that will be, it's early days. There's a lot of stuff building up," he said.
The IMF and other donor nations and agencies agreed on Monday to provide some $16 billion to bail Thailand out of economic woes spawned by collapses in the country's finance and property sectors.
But the process of hammering out the terms of the loan has only just begun, analysts said, and was likely to involve much more than merely hiking the country's Value Added Tax and cutting the budget.

The impact is likely to hurt rich and poor alike, adding to political tensions and a growing sense that Chavalit's government is not up to leading the country through its worst economic crisis in decades, they said.
"We cannot go on like this at this time," said Chira Hongladarom, an academic and former lecturer.
The Thai cabinet is due to consider the details of a cut of between $1.6 billion to $2.3 billion from the budget at its weekly meeting next Tuesday, officials said.
Thais have already started hoarding goods before the three percent VAT hike becomes effective on August 16.
Tuesday's editorials were scathing in their condemnation of the government and gloomy about the immediate future.

"Those who will pay the price range from the wealthy to the poor, the latter group being more vulnerable to retrenchment and overtime cuts in times of economic difficulty," the Bangkok Post wrote in an editorial entitled "The buck stops with all of us".
Overshadowing economics and the IMF issue is the drawing up of a new constitution, which is due to be debated by parliament from September 3.

The assembly charged with drawing up the constitution has enraged several groups, including some 270,000 village heads who have vowed to rally in Bangkok on September 6 to protest against a clause which requires their positions to be elected.
Analysts and diplomats dismissed rumours of an imminent military coup, saying the political landscape no longer tolerated Thailand's oft-used way of changing power.
But others suggested Chavalit may go further than a reshuffle of his cabinet or coalition to appease growing anger.

"Whether we have to go through a bit of a struggle before we get a knight in shining armour, or whether that can be engineered without the struggle, we will know in the course of September," the foreign analyst said.
